They stand particularly in his way and—through their godly meditation, with prayer, fasting, vigils, the <term>mortification of their flesh</term> <note>Original: "Casteyung jres Fleischs," the practice of self-discipline or physical penance to overcome sin</note>, and even through reading, writing, preaching, exhortations, and all kinds of God-pleasing Christian works—they hinder and repel his devilish intent and purpose.

### Preface

Now, however, as the cursed Satan has ever and always raged and stormed against the aforementioned <term>most holy state</term> <note>Original: "Hochheyligen Stand," referring to the religious or monastic life</note>—both by himself and in his own person, as well as through his members and followers—so, on the other hand, Almighty and Merciful God has never allowed it to perish entirely, but has kept a constant seed of it. 

And thus, from the time of the Holy Apostles until now, He has at all times awakened certain prominent holy men who have preserved this blessed state. They have not only protected and defended it with words and deeds, as well as with their spiritual writings, but also with diligence and in all kinds of ways and manners have planted and advanced it. Indeed, they have primarily and most diligently instructed and taught—and partly also recorded with the pen—how and in what manner a truly Christian <term>religious person</term> <note>Original: "Ordens Person," a person belonging to a religious order</note> should primarily be constituted, and what they should do or refrain from. 

Such special, prominent, and fervent zealots of the holy, aforementioned spiritual state and cloistered life have specifically been <term>St. Basil the Great</term> <note>original: "H. ### Preface

For although he founded no new Order, yet after he had devoted himself to the liberal arts in his flourishing youth for seven years in Deventer among the spiritual and devout *Brothers* <note>original: "Fratribus"</note> of the Order of Saint Jerome, and had *progressed* <note>original: "proficiert"</note> very well, and thereafter entered the Order of Saint Augustine—specifically joining the *Canons Regular* <note>original: "Canonicis regularibus," a community of priests living under a rule</note>—he led such a godly, edifying, and holy life in such a *religious state* <note>original: "Religion"; here meaning the monastic life or rule</note> and Order for 71 years (since his entire life extended into his 90th year) that he may well be considered blessed. Not only by his godly conduct and life, but also by his devout, spiritual writings, he gave cause and encouragement to many toward similar godliness and a true Christian monastic life. His magnificent, precious, indeed golden *little works* <note>original: "Opuscula"</note> which he left behind, and which are now found here and there, demonstrate what a zealous, spiritual, and godly man he was.

Therefore, every subject <term>Underthan: a monk or subordinate within the religious order</term> should guard himself against passing insolent judgment <note>original: "freuentliche vrthaile"</note> upon his superior <term>Obern: a higher-ranking official</term> and leader <term>Vorſteher: an overseer or prior</term>. # On Zealous and Fervent Exhortation to the Virtues.
## The First Chapter.

->(Ephesians 4:23)<-

"Be renewed in the spirit of your mind," says the holy Apostle Paul <note>original: "Erneweret euch aber im Geist ewres Gemüets," a citation of Ephesians 4:23</note>. Devout and spiritual members of religious orders <term>Ordens leut: people living in a community under a religious rule, such as monks or nuns</term> are accustomed to practicing good spiritual exercises, through which they are daily awakened to increase in spiritual perfection and the love of virtue. Such people desire nothing other than solitude; they also flee from the common crowds. They examine their lives daily, and if they have perhaps overlooked something in one way or another, they immediately apply themselves to cleansing themselves through proper repentance and sorrow <note>original: "rew vnd leid," terms specifically referring to the theological necessity of contrition and penance</note>.

# On the examination of the
# conscience after Compline.
## The 9th Chapter.

When evening approaches and it grows late, it is fitting that one examines the conscience to see how and in what manner the day has been spent—whether you have been more slothful or more devout. In doing so, if you find any shortcomings in yourself, you should not spare yourself; rather, you should punish your own wickedness, which you have committed, within yourself. You are guilty of such transgressions, for you have done this and that. Reflect on what you did in the choir, or during the office of the <term>Holy Mass</term> <note>original: "h. Meß." # A short exhortation toward spiritual exercise.
## The first chapter:

From external things, one comes to those within; from the lower, one reaches the highest. From the bodily, one moves to the spiritual. A person grows bit by bit, and this occurs through daily exercise <note>vbung: refers here to "spiritual disciplines" or "exercises" like those practiced in a monastery</note>. And although many things may at first seem difficult, these nevertheless become easy and light when they are habituated or pursued. There are three things necessary for every spiritual person, without which a person cannot long persist in a good life. And these are: namely holy prayer, holy reading <term>Lection: from the Latin *lectio*, the practice of meditative, prayerful reading of scripture</term>, and outward work or labor. Within these, one shall—

# The Fifth Book

It is no small or fruitless labor to attend the Choir day and night. Nor is he idle who prays devoutly; indeed, the greatest labor of all is when someone applies himself to prayer even when he feels no desire to pray. Likewise, he is not idle who devotes himself to <term>Holy Scripture</term> <note>original: "H. # Of early night
# waking and rising for Matins.
## The 6th Chapter.

Every midnight, as soon as you are awakened, rise quickly and prepare your heart, so that you may <term>chant psalms</term> <note>original: "pfallierest," from the Latin *psallere*, referring to the liturgical singing or chanting of the Psalms</note> and praise God the Lord with joy and exultation, wakeful and fresh. If you can find no <term>devotion</term> <note>original: "Andacht," a state of focused prayer and spiritual readiness</note> in the Choir, then chant with a fresh spirit and await the <term>grace</term> <note>original: "Genad"</note> of the Lord from heaven. God often grants grace at the end, which he previously—rightly and justly—had denied and withheld from you. He wills that we should labor; he wills that we should patiently await his grace; he further wills that we should make ourselves acceptable and pleasing to him, so that he may grant [it] to us...

<summary>This chapter provides instructions for the midnight prayer service, urging the reader to rise quickly and sing the psalms with a fresh spirit even when feeling a lack of internal devotion. It frames spiritual dryness as a test of patience and labor that God eventually rewards with grace.</summary>
<keywords>Matins, midnight office, spiritual discipline, chanting psalms, divine grace, monastic prayer, persistence</keywords>

...ordained. He wills that we should also fully recognize that we possess nothing good of ourselves, but rather that he extends and gives us all things out of his <term>grace</term> <note>original: "Gnaden"</note> and mercy. Therefore, we should cry out to God our Lord, who created us, and also laud and praise him with singing and music; for there is nothing more pleasant, joyful, nor sweeter than praising God with heart and mouth. May sleep and laziness be far from us and from the place where we stand before the holy angels and before the eyes of the Divine Majesty.

## Concerning Diligent Dwelling
### in the Cells. The 8th Chapter:

After <term>Prime</term> <note>original: "Prim." The first of the "Little Hours" of the Divine Office, observed at sunrise.</note> and <term>Terce</term> <note>original: "Terz." # On the Rejection of External Consolations
## The 16th Chapter

Blessed is he who has no comfort on this earth. Blessed is he who, for Christ’s sake, scorns all temporal <note>original: "zeitlichen". Referring to things belonging to time and the physical world, which are fleeting compared to the eternal.</note> comfort. Blessed also is he who can patiently endure when he is forsaken by God and by men. Blessed also is he who patiently waits upon all of God's providences <term>schickungen: Divine arrangements or the way God disposes of events in a person's life</term>, and willingly accepts all things from His hand. Learn to live without human comfort, even though you might have many who would comfort you. It is a completely vain and unstable comfort when one places his trust and comfort in men, or relies too heavily on their presence <note>original: "zůkunfft". In this context, it refers to the arrival or availability of people to provide support, rather than the "future" in a modern sense.</note>

# The Elder

The **spiritual state** <note>The "clerical" or "monastic" life.</note> is great and also holy, if it is maintained correctly, and if one lives as the **Rules** <note>Referring to the specific monastic rules, such as the Rule of St. Benedict.</note> prescribe and the **monastic habit** <note>The "Ordenkleid" or distinctive clothing of a religious order, which serves as an outward sign of an inward commitment.</note> indicates.
